suggestions.rationale: Systematic-review and meta-analytic evidence reports an association between olfactory impairment and depression, with objective impairment appearing particularly relevant in some subgroups including people with anosmia. This supports focused mental-health review when depression is diagnosed alongside anosmia, but it does not establish direction of effect or an individual medical relationship without chronology, functional-impact evidence, and assessment of other psychiatric and medical contributors.
evidenceGaps: Objective documentation of anosmia or olfactory impairment and its onset
Mental-health records establishing depressive-disorder diagnosis and chronology
Functional and quality-of-life evidence concerning smell loss
Clinical assessment addressing other psychiatric, neurologic, medical, medication, and psychosocial contributors

sourceReferences.citation: Bode et al., Olfactory Impairment and Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis, JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2026. PMID 42424043
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review/meta-analysis of population-based studies reporting associations between subjective/objective olfactory impairment and depression; objective impairment was especially relevant in some subgroups including anosmia. Association does not establish individual direction or causation.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 42424043; abstract; 23 studies representing 17 independent cohorts
